    n=(len(p)-3)//3; y=p[0]+p[1]*(x-2000)/1000+p[2]*((x-2000)/1000)**2

        p[f"x{i}"].set(value=c[0],min=c[1],max=c[2])

observations.finding: Cu: G band at 1580.1–1581.0 cm⁻¹ (±2.6), FWHM 26–30 cm⁻¹, amplitude 24±4 (range 23–26); G amplitude/error ≈ 5.

observations.evidence: Width comparison above; G FWHM 25 (Au) vs 27 (Cu) overlapping within errors.

observations.evidence: I2D/IG amplitude 3.0 (Au) and 2.2 (Cu), FWHM above.

observations.evidence: D amplitude/error ≈ 2.6; ID/IG 0.56–0.64 across variants but with ±0.27 linear error.

properties.source: I2D/IG > 2 and single-Lorentzian 2D; Ferrari et al., PRL 97, 187401, 2006 (from memory, not re-checked).

properties.name: strain_sign
properties.value: none/undetermined — G near 1580–1581 on both; 2D offset of ~15 cm⁻¹ between substrates cannot be assigned to strain or doping without the laser wavelength
properties.source: Lee et al., Nat. Commun. 3, 1024 (2012) for the strain/doping separation method (from memory, not re-checked).

properties.name: doping_type

caveats: The laser wavelength is missing for both files. The 2D position (dispersive, ~90 cm⁻¹/eV) cannot be interpreted absolutely, and the 15 cm⁻¹ Cu–Au offset could be a laser or setup difference rather than material.

Cu signal is about 5–7× weaker than Au and sits on a background hump with ~3× lower relative contrast. Cu G and 2D are real (5σ and ~12σ) but the D band and any D′ are not significant. Any Cu defect or strain number should be treated as unreliable.

Intensity differences between substrates cannot be attributed to layer count, coverage or metal interaction from one spectrum. Candidates: metal-dependent optical enhancement or quenching at the laser wavelength (Au and Cu have different interband absorption in the visible, Johnson & Christy, PRB 6, 4370, 1972, from memory), less graphene coverage within the spot on Cu, different focus on a curved droplet, or a different acquisition setup.

The broad background hump (Au max ~2600 cm⁻¹, Cu max ~1850 cm⁻¹) is not identified. It could be luminescence from carbon contamination, emission from the metal/droplet, or an instrumental artifact. Its origin matters for the interpretation of contrast.

The Au 2D width (41–46 cm⁻¹) is broader than a clean monolayer. This could be strain/doping inhomogeneity across the spot, a few-layer contribution, or the spot covering several grains. One spectrum cannot distinguish these.

Literature values (Ferrari 2006, Cançado 2006/2011, Lee 2012, Giovannetti 2008, Johnson & Christy 1972) are cited from memory; I could not check them here. Use them as pointers, and verify the prefactors before quoting numbers.

Baseline choice affects absolute intensities. ALS (λ=1e5, p=0.01) and local polynomial backgrounds gave consistent positions, but the intensities and I2D/IG depend on the background model, so ratios carry systematic errors larger than the fit errors quoted.

Was a bare Au or bare Cu reference (same laser, power, grating, and integration) measured? This would let the broad background hump be subtracted and tell us whether it is metal emission or carbon luminescence.

What was the spot size, and was the spectrum taken at one point or averaged over the droplet? Was graphene coverage checked by mapping or SEM? A patchy Cu sample would lower the signal without changing the layer quality.

Are the Cu and Au growths comparable in carbon supply and time? The Au sample was grown at high ethylene flux, the Cu sample in UHV, so differences in carbon amount or multilayer patches are possible.
What is the integration time and number of accumulations for each spectrum? This sets the noise (17 vs 8.6 counts) and the detection limit for the Cu D band.
citations: Ferrari, A.C. et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 97, 187401 (2006) — monolayer 2D lineshape, I2D/IG criterion, 2D dispersion (cited from memory, not re-checked)
Cançado, L.G. et al., Appl. Phys. Lett. 88, 163106 (2006) — L_a vs I_D/I_G relation (cited from memory, not re-checked)
Cançado, L.G. et al., Nano Lett. 11, 3190 (2011) — L_D vs I_D/I_G at different excitation energies (cited from memory, not re-checked)
Lee, J.E. et al., Nat. Commun. 3, 1024 (2012) — optical separation of strain and doping via G/2D shift slopes (cited from memory, not re-checked)
Giovannetti, G. et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 101, 026803 (2008) — work-function-dependent doping of graphene by metal contacts (cited from memory, not re-checked)
Johnson, P.B. & Christy, R.W., Phys. Rev. B 6, 4370 (1972) — optical constants of Au and Cu (cited from memory, not re-checked)
limits: Only two spectra, one spot each, no reference spectra, no laser wavelength and no mapping. Layer number and defect spacing are estimates, not measurements.
I did not re-check literature values in this session (no web access); they are from memory and should be verified before use.
Cu D and D′ are not significant, so no defect comparison between the two substrates is possible from these data. The Cu 2D two-component decomposition is unstable and was not used.

The question 'why does it look different' can be answered only partly: intensity and background are measured differences, but their physical causes (metal coupling, coverage, laser/setup) cannot be separated from a single spectrum per substrate.

caveats: The laser wavelength is missing for both files. The 2D position (dispersive, ~90 cm⁻¹/eV) cannot be interpreted absolutely, and the 15 cm⁻¹ Cu–Au offset could be a laser or setup difference rather than material.

Cu signal is about 5–7× weaker than Au and sits on a background hump with ~3× lower relative contrast. Cu G and 2D are real (5σ and ~12σ) but the D band and any D′ are not significant. Any Cu defect or strain number should be treated as unreliable.

Intensity differences between substrates cannot be attributed to layer count, coverage or metal interaction from one spectrum. Candidates: metal-dependent optical enhancement or quenching at the laser wavelength (Au and Cu have different interband absorption in the visible, Johnson & Christy, PRB 6, 4370, 1972, from memory), less graphene coverage within the spot on Cu, different focus on a curved droplet, or a different acquisition setup.

The broad background hump (Au max ~2600 cm⁻¹, Cu max ~1850 cm⁻¹) is not identified. It could be luminescence from carbon contamination, emission from the metal/droplet, or an instrumental artifact. Its origin matters for the interpretation of contrast.

The Au 2D width (41–46 cm⁻¹) is broader than a clean monolayer. This could be strain/doping inhomogeneity across the spot, a few-layer contribution, or the spot covering several grains. One spectrum cannot distinguish these.

Literature values (Ferrari 2006, Cançado 2006/2011, Lee 2012, Giovannetti 2008, Johnson & Christy 1972) are cited from memory; I could not check them here. Use them as pointers, and verify the prefactors before quoting numbers.

Baseline choice affects absolute intensities. ALS (λ=1e5, p=0.01) and local polynomial backgrounds gave consistent positions, but the intensities and I2D/IG depend on the background model, so ratios carry systematic errors larger than the fit errors quoted.
questions_for_user: What laser wavelength was used for each spectrum, and were both measured on the same system and calibration? Without this, the 2D position offset (Cu ~15 cm⁻¹ above Au) and any absolute strain, doping or L_D cannot be assigned.

Was a bare Au or bare Cu reference (same laser, power, grating, and integration) measured? This would let the broad background hump be subtracted and tell us whether it is metal emission or carbon luminescence.

What was the spot size, and was the spectrum taken at one point or averaged over the droplet? Was graphene coverage checked by mapping or SEM? A patchy Cu sample would lower the signal without changing the layer quality.

Are the Cu and Au growths comparable in carbon supply and time? The Au sample was grown at high ethylene flux, the Cu sample in UHV, so differences in carbon amount or multilayer patches are possible.
What is the integration time and number of accumulations for each spectrum? This sets the noise (17 vs 8.6 counts) and the detection limit for the Cu D band.

limits: Only two spectra, one spot each, no reference spectra, no laser wavelength and no mapping. Layer number and defect spacing are estimates, not measurements.
I did not re-check literature values in this session (no web access); they are from memory and should be verified before use.
Cu D and D′ are not significant, so no defect comparison between the two substrates is possible from these data. The Cu 2D two-component decomposition is unstable and was not used.

The question 'why does it look different' can be answered only partly: intensity and background are measured differences, but their physical causes (metal coupling, coverage, laser/setup) cannot be separated from a single spectrum per substrate.
